abstract: Cataract is the leading cause of blindness worldwide. While the oxidative stress homeostasis unbalance of the lens is a key pathological mechanism underlying cataract formation. Due to the lens being deeply embedded behind multiple biological barriers, there is no effective drug treatment for cataract currently. In this study, a multifunctional nanodelivery system (LSPE@Cur) was designed based on cell-penetrating peptide (PENE)-functionalized biomimetic membrane hybrid technology, which prevents cataract by collaboratively regulating mitochondrial homeostasis and oxidative stress balance. The system was constructed by curcumin (Cur)-lipid encapsulation technology combined with PENE functionalization, followed by exosome membrane fusion, creating a biomimetic nanocarrier with long ocular surface retention and deep penetration. This system enables homotypic targeting of lens epithelial cells via exosomal integrins and transmembrane transport proteins, while the PENE's multi-cationic structure ensures precise mitochondrial delivery, establishing a “tissue-organelle” dual-targeting approach. Cur activates the Nrf2 signaling pathway to upregulate the expression of cellular antioxidant enzymes, thereby establishing a long-lasting oxidative defense mechanism. In vitro and in vivo results demonstrated that LSPE@Cur eye drops efficiently maintain lens oxidative stress homeostasis and improve mitochondrial membrane potential. In summary, this study presents an innovative nanomedicine strategy for cataract treatment, offering both efficient delivery and sustained regulation.

2.2
Preparation of biomimetic nanovesicles LSPE@Cur
The synthesis of LSPE@Cur involves three steps. Liposomes loaded with curcumin (LS@Cur) are prepared using the thin-film hydration method: 10 mg of lecithin, 20 mg of DSPE-PEG-COOH, 7.5 mg of cholesterol, and 1 mg of curcumin are dissolved in a chloroform/methanol mixture (10 mL, 2:1 V/V). After the organic solvent is removed by rotary evaporation under reduced pressure, 10 mL of PBS is added to hydrate the lipid film for 30 min, followed by sonication in a water bath for another 30 min. Subsequently, EDC (2 mg) and NHS (2 mg) are added to activate the carboxyl groups for 4 h, after which 6 mg of PENE is added, and the reaction is allowed to continue for an additional 12 h to obtain LSP@Cur. Following the method outlined in the literature, exosomes derived from lens epithelial cells are mixed with LSP@Cur at a protein/phospholipid ratio of 1:5. After 30 min of ice-bath sonication, the mixture is extruded 15 times through a 220 nm polycarbonate membrane using a liposome extruder to obtain the biomimetic nanovesicles, LSPE@Cur. Finally, free drug is removed using a hyperfiltration tube with 30 kDa molecular weight cut-off.
2.3
Characterization of LSPE@Cur
UV–vis spectra were measured using a Shimadzu UV-1780 spectrophotometer, and Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) spectra were acquired with a Nicolet iS20 spectrometer. The concentration of nanovesicles was determined using the Particle Metrix nanoparticle tracking analysis (NTA) system, while the particle size and Zeta potential were analyzed using a Malvern dynamic light scattering (DLS) system. Field emission scanning electron microscopy (FE-SEM) imaging was performed with a Hitachi SU8010 microscope, and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) imaging was carried out using a JEM-1200EX. The in vitro antioxidant activity of LSPE@Cur was evaluated using a total antioxidant capacity assay kit, with absorbance measured at 414 nm. Quantification was based on a Trolox concentration gradient standard curve. The free radical scavenging ability was assessed through the DPPH radical scavenging assay, with absorbance measured at 517 nm. The mucin adhesion characteristics were characterized using a QSense E-Series quartz crystal microbalance combined with a DLS system. Western blot analysis was performed to evaluate the efficiency of exosome isolation and fusion, while dynamic light scattering (DLS) was employed to continuously monitor the zeta potential and hydrodynamic diameter of various nanoplatforms over 14 days to assess their colloidal stability.

2.9
Establishment of animal model
Animal experiments were abided by the law and regulation stipulation and were approved by the Research Ethics Committee of the Eye Hospital of Wenzhou Medical University (Approval No.: YSG25032803). This study established a rat cataract model induced by UVB irradiation. Specifically, SD rats were randomly divided into ten groups (Control, LS@Cur, LSP@Cur, LSE@Cur, LSPE@Cur, UVB + PBS, UVB + LS@Cur, UVB + LSP@Cur, UVB + LSE@Cur and UVB + LSPE@Cur), with 6 eyes per group. 4 h before UVB irradiation, LS@Cur, LSP@Cur, LSE@Cur, LSPE@Cur or PBS solution was instilled into the rats' eyes. The UVB induction process was as follows: rats were anesthetized via intraperitoneal injection of 0.3 mL 2 % sodium pentobarbital, followed by 5 min of topical application of tropicamide solution to dilate the pupils. After pupil dilation, the rats' eyes were exposed to a 312 nm UVB light source (irradiance 800 μW/cm
2

61

Additionally, starting on the third day post-UVB induction, levofloxacin and epithelial growth factor were administered to reduce inflammation and protect the cornea. Eye conditions were observed using a slit-lamp microscope, optical coherence tomography (OCT), and stereomicroscope to assess cataract severity. Based on previously reported quantitative methods, the lens transmittance was measured and quantitatively analyzed, and cataract severity was systematically evaluated according to the LOCS III scoring criteria [
62

Each experiment was independently repeated at least three times, and all data are presented as the mean ± standard deviation (SD). Statistical analyses were performed using Origin 2021 software. All statistical tests were two-tailed, and the sample size for each group is indicated in the figure legends.

Introduction
Cataract is the leading cause of blindness worldwide, primarily characterized by the clouding of the lens, which results in significant vision impairment and severely affects the quality of life of patients [
1
,
2
]. Currently, the only effective treatment for cataracts is phacoemulsification combined with intraocular lens implantation. Although surgical treatment is highly effective, its invasive nature and potential postoperative complications—such as posterior capsule opacification, increased intraocular pressure, and endophthalmitis—underscore the urgent need for non-invasive, safe, and efficient preventive strategies [
[3]
,
[4]
,
[5]
,
[6]
]. Research indicates that the imbalance of oxidative stress homeostasis in the lens plays a crucial role in the development and progression of cataracts. The continuous accumulation of reactive oxygen species (ROS), such as superoxide anion (•O
2
−
), hydroxyl radicals (•OH), and hydrogen peroxide (H
2
O
2
), generated by ultraviolet radiation and endogenous metabolic processes, leads to irreversible damage to lens proteins [
[7]
,
[8]
,
[9]
]. Therefore, maintaining oxidative homeostasis in the lens is a key strategy for preventing cataract formation [
10
,
11
].
Currently, antioxidants such as vitamin C, EGCG, and coenzyme Q10 have garnered significant attention for their promising biomedical applications [
[12]
,
[13]
,
[14]
]. However, few antioxidants have been successfully applied for lens protection to date, largely due to their transient effects and limited efficacy in long-term cataract prevention [
[15]
,
[16]
,
[17]
]. Importantly, natural polyphenols and flavonoids have increasingly become the focus of current research due to their remarkable antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties [
63
,
64
]. Among them, curcumin, a natural polyphenolic compound extracted from turmeric, has attracted particular attention for its unique and potent antioxidant mechanisms. It activates the Nrf2 signaling pathway, upregulating the expression of endogenous antioxidant enzymes, such as superoxide dismutase (SOD), catalase (CAT), and glutathione peroxidase (GPx), thereby enhancing the cellular antioxidant capacity and protecting against oxidative damage [
18
,
19
]. This mechanism makes curcumin a promising candidate for the long-term and efficient prevention of cataracts [
20
,
21
]. Nevertheless, its clinical translation remains constrained by poor water solubility, low bioavailability, and the lack of specific targeting strategies for the lens limits its clinical application. Therefore, overcoming the delivery challenges of curcumin to achieve effective drug accumulation in the lens is a critical challenge in realizing its full preventive potential [
[22]
,
[23]
,
[24]
].
With the continuous development of nanotechnology, drug delivery efficiency for curcumin has been significantly improved. Various nanocarriers have been shown to enhance curcumin's bioavailability effectively [
[25]
,
[26]
,
[27]
,
[28]
]. Exosomes, known for their excellent biocompatibility and integrin-mediated homing targeting ability, have become ideal carriers for drug delivery to the lens. The membrane surface of exosomes is rich in transmembrane proteins and phospholipid domains from homologous cells, enabling efficient recognition and binding to lens epithelial cells [
[29]
,
[30]
,
[31]
]. However, clinical translation of exosomal carriers remains constrained by challenges in scalable production, high costs, and suboptimal drug loading efficiency. Inspired by the synergistic effects of “drug-loaded drug” systems, this study proposes an innovative “carrier-loaded carrier” system, combining the advantages of liposomes and exosomes [
[32]
,
[33]
,
[34]
,
[35]
]. By utilizing the high encapsulation efficiency and established preparation process of liposomes, and integrating the targeting functional domains of exosomes through membrane hybridization, we aim to develop a biomimetic nanovesicle that combines efficient drug loading with precise delivery capabilities [
[36]
,
[37]
,
[38]
]. This system is intended for use as an eye drop formulation for targeted curcumin delivery to the lens.
It is important to note that due to multiple ocular barriers, such as the corneal epithelial tight junctions and tear fluid clearance, eye drop formulations often face challenges with low ocular penetration [
[39]
,
[40]
,
[41]
]. While nanocarriers can effectively enhance drug stability, further functional modifications are necessary to improve drug penetration efficiency [
[42]
,
[43]
,
[44]
,
[45]
]. Studies have shown that cationic modification strategies, such as chitosan and cell-penetrating peptides (CPPs), can enhance drug retention on the ocular surface by adsorbing to the mucous layer of the cornea and temporarily opening epithelial tight junctions to facilitate drug penetration. CPPs, due to their low immunogenicity, high penetration efficiency, and unique functional domains, have garnered significant attention in research [
[46]
,
[47]
,
[48]
]. Notably, PENE peptide (sequence: RQIKIWFQNRRMKWKK) has been proven in several studies to possess excellent cell-penetrating abilities [
49
,
50
]. More importantly, PENE peptide includes a mitochondrial preprotein processing (MPP) enzyme cleavage site (RR) and arginine/lysine-rich domain, which confer mitochondrial targeting potential. When combined with the amphiphilic structure of nanovesicles, PENE peptide holds promise for the precise delivery of curcumin to the mitochondria, thereby reducing oxidative stress damage at its source, maintaining mitochondrial function and oxidative stress homeostasis, and protecting lens epithelial cells [
[51]
,
[52]
,
[53]
].
Herein, we have developed a PENE-functionalized liposome-exosome hybrid biomimetic nanovesicle (LSPE@Cur) for lens-targeted delivery of curcumin, aimed at preventing the onset and progression of cataracts through the remodeling of oxidative stress homeostasis in the lens mediated by the antioxidant curcumin (see
Scheme 1
). Specifically, liposomes were utilized to efficiently encapsulate curcumin, forming a stable nanocarrier system with high bioavailability. To address the lack of specific targeting for the lens, we integrated exosome-mediated homing targeting properties with the “carrier-loaded carrier” strategy, creating a delivery system with both high encapsulation efficiency and lens-targeting ability through liposome-exosome membrane fusion. Considering the multiple ocular barriers anterior to the lens, eye drop formulations frequently encounter penetration challenges including tear clearance and tight junction blockade, resulting in minimal intraocular drug delivery. To overcome this, we employed PENE surface modification to enhance mucin binding and corneal penetration, thus improving the ocular delivery efficiency of the nanocarrier system. Furthermore, the unique amino acid sequence of PENE, in combination with the amphiphilic structure of the nanovesicles, provides the basis for mitochondrial targeting, helping to stabilize mitochondrial function and modulate cellular oxidative stress damage at its source. In vitro and in vivo experiments confirmed that LSPE@Cur, through a three-step adhesion-penetration-targeting delivery pathway, accumulates in the mitochondria of lens epithelial cells, significantly upregulating antioxidant enzymes while coordinately maintaining mitochondrial and oxidative stress homeostasis. This work provides pivotal insights into the development of corneal-penetrating enhanced lens-targeted delivery systems, offering a novel approach for preventive cataract intervention through mitochondrial protection and oxidative stress homeostasis regulation.

Preparation of biomimetic nanovesicles LSPE@Cur
The synthesis of LSPE@Cur involves three steps. Liposomes loaded with curcumin (LS@Cur) are prepared using the thin-film hydration method: 10 mg of lecithin, 20 mg of DSPE-PEG-COOH, 7.5 mg of cholesterol, and 1 mg of curcumin are dissolved in a chloroform/methanol mixture (10 mL, 2:1 V/V). After the organic solvent is removed by rotary evaporation under reduced pressure, 10 mL of PBS is added to hydrate the lipid film for 30 min, followed by sonication in a water bath for another 30 min. Subsequently, EDC (2 mg) and NHS (2 mg) are added to activate the carboxyl groups for 4 h, after which 6 mg of PENE is added, and the reaction is allowed to continue for an additional 12 h to obtain LSP@Cur. Following the method outlined in the literature, exosomes derived from lens epithelial cells are mixed with LSP@Cur at a protein/phospholipid ratio of 1:5. After 30 min of ice-bath sonication, the mixture is extruded 15 times through a 220 nm polycarbonate membrane using a liposome extruder to obtain the biomimetic nanovesicles, LSPE@Cur. Finally, free drug is removed using a hyperfiltration tube with 30 kDa molecular weight cut-off.

3.1
Preparation and characterization of biomimetic nanovesicles LSPE@Cur
LS@Cur nanovesicles were first constructed using the film hydration method, followed by amide coupling to graft PENE onto the vesicle surface to obtain LSP@Cur. Finally, membrane fusion technology was employed to combine Exo with LSP@Cur to form the biomimetic nanovesicles LSPE@Cur [
54
]. Physicochemical characterization showed that both LSPE@Cur and LS@Cur maintained excellent water solubility and exhibited the characteristic UV absorption peak of curcumin at 421 nm, confirming the stable encapsulation of curcumin within the nanocarriers (
Fig. 1
A). FTIR spectral analysis (
Fig. 1
B) revealed PENE modification characteristics: the broad peak in the range of 3200–3600 cm
−1
corresponds to N-H stretching vibrations, a sharp peak at 1750 cm
−1
is attributed to C=O stretching vibrations in carboxyl and amide groups, and a characteristic peak at 1350 cm
−1
reflects symmetric bending vibrations of CH
3
in PENE. The systematic spectral shifts confirmed the successful anchoring of PENE. NTA quantification (
Fig. 1
C and D) showed that the original particle concentration of Exo was 2.9 × 10
10
particles/mL, while the particle concentrations of LSP@Cur and LSPE@Cur reached 2.2 × 10
11
particles/mL. In fluorescence mode, DiO-labeled Exo maintained a signal of 2.7 × 10
10
particles/mL, while LSP@Cur without fluorescence labeling showed no detectable signal. LSPE@Cur, derived from membrane fusion, exhibited 1.8 × 10
11
particles/mL of fluorescent positive particles, significantly higher than the signal from free Exo, further confirming the successful integration of Exo membrane proteins onto the LSP@Cur surface during the membrane fusion process. In addition, zeta potential analysis revealed significant interfacial electrochemical reorganization: The surface potential of LS@Cur was −7.8 ± 0.35 mV. After modification with PENE, the potential of LSP@Cur shifted significantly in the positive direction to −2.0 ± 0.3 mV (Δζ = +5.8 mV, p < 0.001), which is attributed to the positive charge contribution from the amine groups in the PENE molecular chain. Compared to LSE@Cur, LSPE@Cur also exhibited a similar increase in surface potential. The 2.8 mV potential difference (p < 0.04) between LSP@Cur and LSPE@Cur further confirmed that the integration of exosomal membrane proteins led to surface charge redistribution (
Fig. 1
E). Surface morphology analysis showed that SEM images (
Fig. 1
F) of all five types of nanovesicles revealed typical spherical structures with good dispersion. TEM negative staining (
Fig. 1
G) indicated that all particles exhibited the characteristic phospholipid bilayer ultrastructure. The dried particle size of Exo was approximately 50 nm, while the other four nanovesicles had a particle size around 100 nm. DLS analysis showed that the hydrodynamic diameter of Exo was primarily concentrated around 100 nm, while the other four nanovesicles exhibited a broader size distribution ranging from 100 to 300 nm. The stability of the 4 nanocarrier systems was continuously monitored by DLS over a 14-day period. Notably, the Exo exhibited fluctuations in both zeta potential and particle size on day 4, whereas the other three systems remained relatively stable throughout the observation period. In particular, LSPE@Cur did not display similar instability despite the incorporation of exosomal fragments. This enhanced stability is likely attributed to the excellent structural integrity of the liposomes, which effectively anchor the exosomal components onto the nanocarrier surface (
Fig. S1
).

Conclusion
In summary, this study successfully developed a biomimetic drug delivery system, LSPE@Cur, based on hybrid nanovesicles functionalized with cell-penetrating peptides and loaded with curcumin. By integrating mucin-affinity PENE and amphiphilic nanocarriers, the system effectively achieves a synergistic “corneal adhesion-barrier penetration” effect. The abundant integrin proteins and transmembrane transporters on the exosome membrane provide reliable homologous targeting for the drug delivery system. The unique amino acid sequence of PENE, which includes mitochondrial precursor protein (MPP) cleavage sites and a high density of cationic arginine/lysine residues, endows the system with spatiotemporally controllable mitochondrial targeting ability. More importantly, curcumin exhibits an outstanding antioxidant mechanism by effectively activating the Nrf2 signaling pathway, which enhances the expression of antioxidant enzymes in lens epithelial cells. This, in turn, strengthens their intrinsic resistance to oxidative stress and facilitates the establishment of a stable, long-lasting, and highly efficient antioxidant defense system. This system demonstrates significant potential for precise drug delivery, reducing the frequency of administration, and offering long-term prevention of cataracts. Both in vitro and in vivo experiments show that LSPE@Cur exhibits excellent biocompatibility and overcomes the limitations of traditional eye drops, such as poor ocular retention and low lens drug accumulation. Within cells, it provides ideal mitochondrial targeting capabilities. Through activation of the Nrf2 signaling pathway, enhanced antioxidant enzyme expression, ROS scavenging, and maintenance of mitochondrial homeostasis, LSPE@Cur offers comprehensive protection to lens epithelial cells, shielding them from oxidative stress. Moreover, the “structural biomimicry-functional synergy-mechanism complementarity” design strategy introduces a new paradigm for the development of ocular tissue-targeted delivery systems, demonstrating important value in translational medicine and preclinical research. Although cortical cataract is the most common type observed clinically and is generally believed to result from an imbalance in lens oxidative stress homeostasis induced by ultraviolet radiation and endogenous metabolic factors, numerous studies suggest that age-related nuclear cataracts are primarily triggered by senescence-associated factors released during the chronic aging process rather than by oxidative stress alone. In the present study, LSPE@Cur demonstrated promising protective effects only in a UVB-induced cortical cataract rat model caused by oxidative stress. However, its efficacy has not yet been evaluated in primate models, nor has it been investigated in cataracts induced by other factors, such as senescence-associated nuclear cataracts.
